Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. REFERENCE NOTES

Harbor Window Food Cooperative serves about 430 member households from a small storefront and a weekly neighborhood pickup site in Bellwether. The inventory review concerns the week of October 14. Inventory lead Nia Calder coordinates counts with receiving volunteer Tomas Ibarra and produce manager Elise Park. The cooperative uses a shared spreadsheet called Stockbook, but delivery records are also kept on paper until the receiving shift has checked each shipment. The team wants a review plan that fits its regular shifts rather than requiring a special all-day closure.

On Monday morning, Tomas received 24 crates of North Fork pears and wrote 24 on the paper receiving sheet. The driver’s signed ticket says 24, but the Stockbook entry shows 22. Nia has not yet matched the entry against the signed ticket or checked whether two crates were entered under the pickup-site transfer. The pears are in the north walk-in, on pallet P-3, with lot code NF-1014. Elise said, “Let’s count the pallet before anyone changes the sheet; I don’t want a guess becoming the official number.” The produce team has a scheduled receiving-and-count shift from 8:00 to 10:00 a.m. Monday, and the walk-in can be counted without moving the other pallets.

If the difference is resolved against the signed receiving ticket and the physical count by 10:00 a.m. Monday, update Stockbook to the verified crate count and assign the pears to the normal shelf and pickup allocation. If the difference is not resolved by 10:00 a.m. Monday, leave the recorded count unchanged, flag the line as unresolved, and keep the affected pear lot out of sale until Nia reviews the paper transfer record. Neither branch authorizes estimating a count. The shift lead should note who checked the ticket, the pallet, and the transfer record, and when the line was updated or flagged.

The north walk-in temperature logger recorded 3.6°C at 6:00 a.m. Monday. Its prior reading, taken at 6:00 p.m. Sunday, was 3.8°C, and the target range posted on the door is 1–4°C. Elise saw no damaged crates during the initial receiving check, but she has not inspected the bottom layer of the pear pallet. The thermometer display is readable, and a spare logger is stored in the office drawer beside the receiving clipboard. If a later logger check shows a reading outside the posted range, the shift lead should record the reading and time and tell Nia before the affected lot is moved to the pickup site. The notes do not establish that a temperature excursion occurred.

The co-op has 18 reusable produce totes at the pickup site and 11 clean totes in the storefront stockroom. Tomas counted the pickup-site totes after Sunday pickup, while Elise counted the stockroom totes before opening Monday. Two totes returned from the Saturday market still need washing; they are beside the utility sink and should not be counted as clean stock. The tote shelf label says “30 minimum for Thursday pickup,” but there is no separate tote purchase order. Nia asked the team to record clean, used, and awaiting-wash totes separately so that the Thursday allocation is based on usable stock, not the total number of containers in the building.

1. Monday review sequence
   - Compare the pear entry in Stockbook with the signed delivery ticket and the paper transfer record.
   - Count pallet P-3 and record the lot code, verified quantity, checker, and check time.
   - Apply the appropriate conditional action above; do not replace an unresolved count with an estimate.
   - Check the walk-in logger and inspect the bottom layer of the pallet before any transfer to the pickup site.
   - Count clean totes by location and list the two awaiting-wash totes separately.

The dry-goods shelf also needs a count before the Thursday pickup forecast is prepared. Stockbook lists 36 jars of Red Lantern tomato sauce, while the shelf count on Sunday evening was 31. Three jars were set aside in a clearly marked box for a member order, and two jars were used for the October 12 cooking demonstration; the demonstration slip is clipped to the weekly sales sheet but has not been entered in Stockbook. Aisha Venn, who closes the storefront on Sundays, wrote, “I put the three member jars in the blue order crate, not on the regular shelf.” The team should distinguish reserved stock from stock available for general sale and check the demonstration slip before changing the ledger. The member order is due for pickup Wednesday, so the reserved jars should remain assigned to that order unless the order record itself shows a change.

For the produce forecast, Elise expects 16 pear crates to be available for regular sales if the count is verified and no lot hold applies. The pickup coordinator has requested 10 crates for Thursday and the storefront normally keeps at least four crates for walk-in shoppers. Those figures are planning requests, not proof that the stock is available. If the unresolved-count branch remains in effect, or if the pear lot is held after a logger check, do not include the affected pears in the Thursday promotion forecast. If the count is verified and no lot hold applies, Nia may use the 16-crate planning figure to check whether the pickup request and the four-crate storefront minimum fit; she should record any shortfall rather than silently reducing either request. The Thursday email draft is due Wednesday at noon, after the Tuesday morning inventory review.

Nia also wants the final review notes to identify which entries were checked, which remain unresolved, and the next person responsible for each follow-up. Tomas is on receiving duty Tuesday from 8:00 to 9:30 a.m.; Elise can inspect produce before the storefront opens at 9:00 a.m.; Aisha is not scheduled again until Wednesday afternoon. The cooperative’s weekly member bulletin should not state that a discrepancy has been corrected unless Stockbook and the supporting record have actually been checked. The records available for this review are the Stockbook export, Monday’s signed pear ticket, the paper transfer record, the logger readings, the tote counts, the marked member-order crate, and the demonstration slip.

On Tuesday afternoon, the inventory lead will review the Monday notes with the receiving and produce teams before the Wednesday email is drafted. The final review should keep the difference between verified quantities, reserved goods, and goods on hold visible to anyone preparing the pickup list. Any update made after the Monday count should include its source and timestamp, so a later reader can tell whether it came from a physical recount, a delivery record, or a transfer entry. The team has not yet made a decision about purchasing additional totes or changing the Thursday pickup request; those questions can be recorded for follow-up, but the review should not treat either as approved.", "output": "Create a practical review and follow-up plan for Harbor Window Food Cooperative’s inventory lead, using the reference notes below. Organize the plan around the Monday inventory review, the Tuesday follow-up, and preparation of the Wednesday email. Identify the records and people relevant to each step, and distinguish verified quantities, reserved goods, unresolved counts, and goods on hold.

Preserve the conditional actions for the pear count: when the difference is resolved by 10:00 a.m. Monday, use the verified count and assign the pears to normal shelf and pickup allocation; when it is not resolved by then, leave the recorded count unchanged, flag the line, and keep the affected lot out of sale until Nia reviews the paper transfer record. Do not estimate a count. Keep the later Thursday promotion decision conditional on the count being verified and no lot hold applying; do not include affected pears in the forecast if the unresolved-count branch remains in effect or the lot is held. Treat planning figures and requests as such, not as confirmed availability or approval. Do not imply that a discrepancy, temperature excursion, or other issue has been resolved unless the notes establish it.

Organize the response so the inventory lead can follow the sequence, record findings and ownership, and see what remains open. Include the numbered Monday review sequence and account for the source records, time constraints, tote categories, reserved tomato sauce, logger check, and Tuesday review.
